# Background and Rationale

## An Insight into Motivations, Effects, and Therapeutic Potentials

The contemporary landscape of mental health and psychological well-being is characterised by a growing recognition that conventional, pathology-driven therapeutic models—while undeniably effective for severe psychiatric disorders—are insufficient on their own to address the full spectrum of human distress, stress, and psychological stagnation. As the prevalence of anxiety, depressive episodes, burnout, and post-traumatic stress continues to rise across global populations, scholars, clinicians, and policy-makers have increasingly turned their attention to complementary, expressive, and experiential modalities that harness the body, the creative impulse, and the reflective self as agents of healing. Against this backdrop, the present dissertation situates its investigation at the intersection of motivational psychology, behavioural and physiological outcome research, and therapeutic outcome literature, seeking to generate a more unified and empirically grounded understanding of why individuals gravitate toward certain expressive or somatic practices, what measurable and subjective effects those practices produce, and to what extent those effects can be harnessed within a formal therapeutic framework. The following items outline the specific strands of background, contextual justification, and rationale that motivate and shape this study.

!!?? The field of health and social psychology has long documented that individuals do not engage in wellness-oriented or expressive activities in a vacuum; rather, their participation is governed by a complex matrix of intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, ranging from hedonic pleasure and aesthetic curiosity to the desire for social belonging, identity construction, emotional regulation, and, in some cases, a conscious or unconscious attempt to manage pre-existing psychological difficulties (Deci & Ryan, 2000; Vallerand, 2001). Despite the wealth of self-report survey data on leisure and creative activities, comparatively little research has disentangled these motivational layers specifically within populations who are at the threshold of clinical distress or who are actively seeking therapeutic support. This gap limits clinicians' ability to tailor interventions to a client's self-perceived "reason for doing," a factor that emerging implementation-science literature suggests is a critical predictor of engagement, adherence, and ultimate therapeutic gain.

!!?? Parallel to the motivational question lies the empirical question of effects. Over the past two decades, a substantial but still fragmented body of literature has documented the acute and chronic effects of expressive, creative, and somatic practices on a range of psychobiological indicators: reductions in salivary and serum cortisol, modulation of autonomic nervous system activity (heart-rate variability, skin conductance), shifts in brain-region activation patterns (notably in the default-mode network, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala), alterations in inflammatory cytokine profiles, and subjective improvements in mood, self-efficacy, and perceived coherence (Baker et al., 2018; Park, 2014; Loman & Priebe, 2012). However, the heterogeneity of methodologies—cross-sectional designs, small convenience samples, variable control conditions, and inconsistent primary outcome measures—prevents a clear, integrative picture from emerging. This dissertation therefore positions itself as a synthetic and exploratory contribution that brings together psychometric, physiological, and qualitative evidence streams to map the effect landscape more systematically.

!!?? The third pillar of the study—the therapeutic potential—raises the question of translational validity: can the well-being and symptom-relief effects observed in community or recreational settings be reliably reproduced, amplified, and ethically framed within a clinical or semi-clinical therapeutic context? The World Health Organization (2022) and the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health have both called for robust evidence on the integration of expressive and somatic modalities into multidisciplinary care pathways, yet most existing trials suffer from limited sample sizes, short follow-up windows, and a tendency to conflate "wellness benefit" with "therapeutic efficacy." A rigorous delineation of when an effect constitutes a genuine therapeutic mechanism (e.g., exposure, narrative re-processing, embodied regulation) versus a passive or placebo-like relief is essential for responsible clinical integration and for avoiding the dilution of evidence-based practice.

!!?? A further layer of background that informs this project is the socio-cultural and economic context in which individuals encounter these practices. In many high-income and increasingly middle-income societies, expressive and somatic activities have become commodified through digital platforms, boutique wellness industries, and social-media-driven "self-care" narratives. This commercialisation can simultaneously democratise access and distort motivation, as participants may be driven less by authentic psychological need and more by performative, identity-signalling, or peer-comparison dynamics (Munoz et al., 2013; Varga & Carr, 2014). Understanding this motivational contamination is critical for any therapeutic application, because an intervention embedded in a consumerist framework may fail to address the deeper regulatory and integrative needs of a clinically vulnerable individual.

!!?? From a theoretical standpoint, this dissertation draws on several complementary frameworks: self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness) to parse motivational architecture; affect regulation and the polyvagal theory (Porges, 2011) to model physiological and emotional effects; narrative and meaning-making theory (McAdams, 2001) to interpret the cognitive-experiential processing that occurs during expressive engagement; and the biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) as an overarching integrative lens. No single framework adequately captures the multi-systemic nature of the phenomenon under study, and the rationale for employing a multi-theoretical, mixed-methods design is that the interplay between motivation, effect, and therapeutic potential is inherently cross-level and non-reducible to one domain of explanation.

!!?? Methodologically, the background of this project is informed by the growing acceptance and refinement of mixed-methods and participatory research designs in health psychology and psychotherapy research. While randomised controlled trials remain the gold standard for efficacy questions, they are poorly suited to capturing the subjective, temporal, and context-sensitive dimensions of motivational experience and perceived therapeutic meaning. Convergent parallel mixed-methods designs—pairing validated psychometric instruments and, where feasible, basic physiological measurement with semi-structured interviews or focus groups—allow the researcher to triangulate quantitative effect sizes with rich, process-oriented qualitative data. The rationale for this methodological choice is that the research questions ("why do people do this?", "what do they experience?", "does it function therapeutically?") are, by their nature, multi-dimensional and require more than a single methodological family to answer satisfactorily.

!!?? Ethical and epistemological considerations form an additional strand of rationale. Investigative work at the intersection of mental health, embodied practice, and potential therapeutic application raises important questions about research ethics: informed consent for physiological monitoring, the risk of re-traumatisation when participants are asked to narrate distressing experiences, the responsibility of the researcher not to imply unvalidated therapeutic claims to vulnerable participants, and the careful handling of data that may reveal sensitive mental-health status. The background for this project therefore includes a commitment to reflexive, participatory, and transparent research practice, grounded in the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, institutional ethics review, and the emerging field of research ethics in complementary and integrative health (Booth et al., 2018). The rationale is both protective (safeguarding participants) and epistemological: ethical rigour strengthens the credibility and generalisability of the findings.

!!?? The timeliness of this investigation is underscored by several converging trends. First, the post-pandemic surge in demand for accessible, low-cost, and self-directed mental-health support has placed expressive and somatic practices at the centre of public discourse, yet the evidence base has not kept pace with public enthusiasm. Second, the ongoing crisis in therapist supply and accessibility in many health systems has intensified interest in "therapeutic potential" as a property that can extend beyond the four walls of a clinical office into community, digital, and peer-supported settings. Third, recent advances in psychoneuroimmunology, wearable biosensing, and mobile-based data collection have made it feasible to capture fine-grained, real-time physiological and behavioural data that were previously confined to laboratory settings. This dissertation leverages these methodological advances to produce findings that are both empirically rigorous and ecologically valid.

!!?? Finally, the broader rationale for this project is rooted in a conviction that the current literature tends to treat motivation, effect, and therapeutic potential as three separate research questions pursued by three separate communities of scholars (leisure studies, health psychology, and clinical psychotherapy, respectively). In reality, these three dimensions are tightly coupled: the motivation with which a person engages in a practice shapes the depth and quality of the effect they experience, and the nature of that effect, in turn, either reinforces or undermines the perceived therapeutic value of the practice over time. A failure to study this coupling in an integrated fashion risks producing a body of knowledge that is fragmented, internally contradictory, and of limited practical utility for both practitioners and policy-makers. This dissertation aims to bridge that gap by positioning motivation, effect, and therapeutic potential as co-constitutive components of a single, dynamic system, and by generating data that speak to all three simultaneously.

In sum, the background and rationale outlined above justify the present study as a necessary, timely, and methodologically coherent contribution to an area of research that is expanding rapidly in public relevance but remains under-theorised and under-integrated in the academic literature. The project aspires to produce findings that are theoretically grounded, empirically substantiated, ethically responsible, and directly translatable into improved therapeutic practice, policy guidance, and future research agendas.
